claims.text: A machine-learning approach integrating bulk composition with atomic size disorder, configurational entropy, and local lattice distortion can predict low phonon thermal conductivity in single-phase high-entropy alloys more accurately than composition-only models.
Conventional predictive models for high-entropy-alloy thermal conductivity rely largely on bulk composition averages.
Arc melting followed by homogenization ensures a uniform, single-phase solid solution in the proposed high-entropy alloys.
Fine-scale microstructural features can be incorporated with bulk composition to estimate phonon scattering and thermal conductivity.
Local lattice distortions and atomic-level disorder govern phonon-scattering mechanisms relevant to lowering thermal conductivity.
A richer feature set captures contributions from local vibrational modes and inhomogeneities to phonon scattering.
Capturing local vibrational modes and microstructural inhomogeneities permits more precise prediction of reduced thermal conductivity.
Bulk-averaged conventional methods overlook thermal-conductivity-relevant microstructural variations.
The enhanced method will reduce phonon-thermal-conductivity prediction error by roughly 20% relative to conventional models.
The enhanced method will improve identification of high-entropy alloys having low thermal conductivity.
Current composition-focused approaches produce higher phonon-thermal-conductivity prediction errors because they omit detailed microstructural characteristics.
The approach is expected to be effective only for homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloys.
Significant phase separation or non-uniform microstructures may reduce the approach's accuracy.
Multiphase alloys may contain scattering mechanisms not represented by the approach.
Compositions that deviate strongly from the training data may fall outside the approach's reliable domain.
The experimental benchmark compares errors from the enhanced and conventional models against room-temperature transient-laser-flash measurements on homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloys.
Failure to achieve at least a 20% reduction in prediction error relative to conventional models falsifies the hypothesis.
Failure of measured thermal conductivities to align with the predicted low-conductivity range also falsifies the hypothesis.
